question: A seller left a large mirror bolted to the bathroom wall and did not mention it in the sales contract. Under the common-law test for fixtures, which factor is generally given the MOST weight in determining whether the mirror stays with the property?
choice_a: The method and permanence of attachment to the real property
choice_b: The original purchase price of the item
choice_c: The color and style of the item
choice_d: Whether the item was purchased before or after the mortgage was recorded
explanation: Courts typically weigh several factors (method of attachment, adaptation to the property, agreement of the parties, and intention/relationship of the parties, sometimes remembered as MARIA), but the manner and permanence of attachment is the most commonly cited and heavily weighted test for whether an item has become a fixture and thus real property.

question: A tenant installed specialized display shelving in a rented retail space to conduct her business. When the lease ends, which statement about this shelving is TRUE?
choice_a: It automatically becomes the landlord's real property the moment it is installed
choice_b: It is a trade fixture and the tenant may remove it before the lease expires
choice_c: It must remain because all attached items are permanent fixtures
choice_d: It converts to personal property only if the tenant pays a removal fee
explanation: Trade fixtures are items a commercial tenant installs to conduct business; despite being attached, they remain the tenant's personal property and may be removed before the lease term ends, provided the tenant repairs any damage caused by removal.

question: A farmer sells his land but has an unharvested wheat crop still in the field at closing. Absent a contrary agreement, how is the standing, cultivated crop classified?
choice_a: A fixture that automatically transfers with the land
choice_b: An encumbrance on the new owner's title
choice_c: Emblements, treated as personal property belonging to the farmer
choice_d: Real property that cannot be severed from the land
explanation: Annually cultivated crops (emblements) are considered personal property (chattel), even though they are attached to the land, and generally belong to the party who planted and cultivated them unless the parties agree otherwise.

question: Which document is used to convey ownership of personal property, as distinguished from the document used to convey real property?
explanation: A bill of sale transfers title to personal property (chattel), while a deed is the instrument used to convey title to real property. Distinguishing which instrument applies is essential when a transaction includes both a home and, for example, furniture or equipment.

question: A deeded parking space and storage unit are described in a condominium deed as passing automatically with ownership of the unit. What term best describes this kind of right?
explanation: An appurtenance is a right, privilege, or improvement that belongs to and passes with the land or unit, such as an easement, a deeded parking space, or water rights, even though it may not be physically part of the property itself.

question: The legal concept describing real property ownership as a collection of separate legal rights — including the rights to possess, use, transfer, encumber, and exclude others — is best known as the:
explanation: The bundle of rights concept views ownership not as a single right but as a collection of individual rights that can be separated and conveyed independently, such as selling mineral rights while retaining surface rights.

question: Which best distinguishes real property from personal property?
choice_a: Real property includes only buildings, while personal property includes land
choice_b: Real property is always owned by a business entity, while personal property is only owned by individuals
choice_c: Real property is land and everything permanently attached to it plus the rights of ownership, while personal property is movable and not permanently affixed
choice_d: There is no legal distinction; the terms are interchangeable
explanation: Real property (realty) consists of land, everything permanently attached to it (improvements and fixtures), and the legal rights of ownership. Personal property (personalty or chattel) is anything movable that is not permanently affixed to the land.

question: A legal description that begins at a point of beginning and traces a parcel's boundary using directions, distances, and physical monuments back to that same point is known as:
explanation: The metes and bounds method describes a parcel's boundaries using courses (directions), distances, and monuments (natural or artificial markers), starting and ending at a defined point of beginning, and is one of the oldest surveying methods still used today.

question: A subdivision developer records a plat map showing individual parcels identified by number within numbered blocks. Deeds for those parcels can then simply reference the recorded map. This method of legal description is called:
choice_a: The lot and block (recorded plat) system
explanation: The lot and block system, also called the recorded plat method, describes property by referencing a lot number and block number shown on a subdivision plat map that has been recorded in the county's public records.

question: The rectangular (government) survey system establishes location by referencing the intersection of which two reference lines?
choice_a: A township line and a range line only
choice_b: A principal meridian (running north-south) and a base line (running east-west)
choice_c: A point of beginning and a monument
explanation: The government (rectangular) survey system, used in most of the United States, establishes a grid based on principal meridians running north-south and base lines running east-west; townships and ranges are then measured from the intersection of these lines.

question: Under the government (rectangular) survey system, a standard township is a square parcel measuring approximately how large, and how many sections does it contain?
explanation: A township under the government survey system is a square roughly 6 miles by 6 miles, totaling 36 square miles, and is divided into 36 numbered sections, each approximately 1 mile square.

question: One section of land in the government (rectangular) survey system contains how many acres?
explanation: A section is one square mile and contains 640 acres. Sections are often further divided into halves, quarters, and quarter-quarters for smaller parcel descriptions (for example, a quarter section equals 160 acres).

question: A rectangular lot measures 200 feet by 217.8 feet. Approximately how many acres is this lot, given that one acre equals 43,560 square feet?
explanation: 200 feet multiplied by 217.8 feet equals 43,560 square feet, which is exactly one acre. Knowing that an acre equals 43,560 square feet is essential for converting between square footage and acreage.

question: A surveyor needs a permanent reference point of known location and elevation to establish measurements for a new survey. This reference point is called a:
explanation: A benchmark is a permanent reference marker of known location and elevation, established by a surveyor, that is used as a starting point for future surveys and elevation measurements, distinct from a datum, which is the reference plane itself.

question: A condominium unit occupying the fourteenth floor of a high-rise building is legally described using boundaries defined by elevation above a fixed reference plane rather than by ground boundaries. This type of legal description is called a(n):
explanation: An air lot is a parcel of airspace above the surface of the land, described by reference to a datum (elevation reference plane), and is commonly used to legally describe condominium units and airspace ownership in multi-story buildings.

question: Which physical characteristic of land explains why no two parcels of real property are ever exactly identical, even if they are the same size and shape?
explanation: Nonhomogeneity, also called uniqueness or nonhomogeneity of location, means every parcel of land occupies a distinct geographic location, so no two parcels are ever truly identical. This is why real estate law recognizes the remedy of specific performance for land sale contracts.

question: A claim, charge, or liability attached to real property that may diminish its value or restrict its use, but does not necessarily prevent transfer of title, is generally known as a(n):
explanation: An encumbrance is any claim, charge, or liability that attaches to real property, such as a lien, easement, or restriction. Encumbrances can affect value or use, but the property can typically still be conveyed subject to them.

question: A lien is best defined as which of the following?
choice_a: A right to use another person's land for a specific purpose
choice_b: A charge or claim against a property that secures payment of a debt or obligation
choice_c: A physical intrusion of a structure onto a neighboring lot
choice_d: A restriction on how a property may be used, created by private agreement
explanation: A lien is a specific type of encumbrance that gives a creditor a legal claim against property as security for the payment of a debt or performance of an obligation, such as a mortgage lien or a tax lien.

question: A judgment lien resulting from a lawsuit against a property owner typically attaches to which of the following?
choice_a: Only the one specific property named in the lawsuit, making it a specific lien
choice_b: Only personal property, never real property
choice_c: All real and personal property the debtor owns in that county, making it a general lien
choice_d: Nothing until the debtor sells the property
explanation: A judgment lien is a general lien, meaning it attaches to all property, both real and personal, that the debtor owns within the jurisdiction where the judgment is recorded, unlike a specific lien (such as a mortgage), which attaches to only one identified property.

question: An unpaid contractor who performed work on a homeowner's property can file which type of lien to secure payment for labor and materials provided?
explanation: A mechanic's lien allows contractors, subcontractors, and suppliers who provide labor or materials to improve real property to file a claim against that property if they are not paid, and in many jurisdictions its priority can relate back to the date the work began.

question: Among competing liens against a property, which lien generally holds the highest priority regardless of its recording date?
explanation: Real property tax liens (and special assessment liens) are generally given superior priority over virtually all other liens against a property, even those recorded earlier, because governments need reliable tax revenue to fund public services.

question: A neighbor has used a paved path across an adjoining owner's backyard for years to reach a lake, and this right was granted in writing and recorded so it benefits whichever lot the neighbor owns. This is an example of what type of easement?
choice_a: An easement in gross, which is a personal right unrelated to any parcel of land
choice_b: An easement appurtenant, which runs with the land and involves a dominant and servient estate
choice_c: A license, which can be revoked at will
explanation: An easement appurtenant benefits a specific parcel of land (the dominant estate) and burdens another parcel (the servient estate). It runs with the land, meaning it transfers automatically to new owners when either property is sold.

question: A utility company holds a recorded right to run power lines across a private landowner's property. Because this right benefits the utility company itself rather than a neighboring parcel of land, it is classified as a(n):
explanation: An easement in gross benefits a specific person or entity rather than a neighboring parcel of land, so there is no dominant estate. Utility easements are a common example and are typically assignable and do not require adjoining land ownership.

question: A parcel of land becomes landlocked after a larger tract is subdivided, leaving it with no access to a public road except across a neighboring lot. A court may grant which type of easement to provide access?
explanation: An easement by necessity is created by a court when a landlocked parcel has no legal access to a public road, typically arising when a larger tract was divided and one resulting parcel lost all access without crossing another lot.

question: A hiker has openly and continuously crossed a private, unfenced field on a well-worn trail for the statutory period required by state law, without the landowner's permission. The hiker may be able to claim what kind of easement as a result?
explanation: An easement by prescription is acquired through open, notorious, continuous, and hostile (non-permissive) use of another's land for the period of time set by state statute, similar to adverse possession but granting only a right of use rather than title.

question: A homeowner gives a neighbor verbal permission to park a boat trailer on a portion of her driveway temporarily. This type of permission, which can be revoked at any time and does not run with the land, is called a:
explanation: A license is a personal, revocable permission to use another's land for a specific purpose. Unlike an easement, a license is not considered an interest in real property, does not run with the land, and can be terminated by the landowner at will.

question: A new survey reveals that a homeowner's fence and a corner of her garage extend eighteen inches onto the adjoining lot. This physical intrusion of a structure onto a neighbor's property is called a(n):
explanation: An encroachment occurs when a structure, fence, driveway, or other improvement unlawfully extends onto an adjoining owner's property, and it is commonly discovered through a boundary survey performed before closing.

question: A person can acquire legal title to another's land without paying for it if the person's possession of the land meets which set of common-law requirements over the statutory period?
choice_a: Possession that is secret and permissive
choice_b: Payment of the property's real estate taxes only, with no physical possession required
choice_c: A single season of occupancy with the landowner's written consent
choice_d: Open, notorious, continuous, and hostile (adverse) possession, often also requiring exclusivity
explanation: Adverse possession allows a person to gain legal title to land by possessing it openly, notoriously, continuously, and hostilely (without the owner's permission) for a period of time set by state statute; many states also require the possession to be exclusive and, in some cases, that taxes be paid.

question: An owner sells the surface rights to a tract of farmland but retains the right to extract coal, oil, and gas from beneath the property. This illustrates that which category of property rights can be severed and conveyed separately from surface ownership?
explanation: Mineral (subsurface) rights, which include the right to extract oil, gas, coal, and other minerals below the surface, can be severed from the surface estate and owned or sold separately, illustrating the bundle-of-rights concept.

question: An owner whose land borders a non-navigable stream generally has rights to reasonable use of the water flowing past the property, shared with other landowners along the same waterway. These rights are known as:
explanation: Riparian rights apply to owners of land bordering flowing waterways such as rivers and streams, giving them reasonable use of the water. Littoral rights, by contrast, apply to land bordering large, non-flowing bodies of water such as lakes, seas, or oceans.

question: In several western states, water rights are allocated according to a doctrine under which the first person to put water to beneficial use has a superior claim to it, regardless of whether their land actually borders the water source. This is known as:
explanation: The prior appropriation doctrine, used primarily in arid western states, allocates water rights based on who first put the water to beneficial use ('first in time, first in right'), independent of whether the water user's land is adjacent to the water source.

question: A landowner sells the right to build and use the space above her single-story building to a developer, who plans to construct additional floors above it. This transaction involves which property right?
explanation: Air rights are the rights to use, control, and occupy the vertical space above a parcel of land. Like mineral rights, air rights can be severed from the land and sold or leased separately, which occurs in dense urban development and transferable development rights programs.

question: A single unmarried individual takes title to a home entirely in her own name, with no co-owners. This form of ownership is known as ownership in:
explanation: Ownership in severalty means title is held by a single person or single legal entity, severed from all others. Despite the word 'several' suggesting multiple owners, it actually refers to sole ownership.

question: Three unrelated investors purchase an office building together. Each owns a distinct, undivided interest that need not be equal, each may sell or will their share independently, and there is no automatic right of survivorship. This describes:
explanation: Tenancy in common allows two or more owners to hold undivided interests in a property, which may be unequal in size. Each co-tenant can freely transfer or will their interest, and upon death an interest passes to the deceased owner's heirs rather than automatically to the other co-owners.

question: For a valid joint tenancy to be created at common law, the co-owners' interests must satisfy the four unities. Which of the following correctly lists these four unities?
explanation: The four unities required for a common-law joint tenancy are unity of time (interests acquired at the same time), title (acquired through the same document), interest (equal ownership shares), and possession (equal right to possess the whole property). Joint tenancy also carries the right of survivorship.

question: Two siblings hold title to a vacation home as joint tenants with right of survivorship. If one sibling dies, what happens to that sibling's ownership interest?
choice_a: It passes to the deceased sibling's heirs according to a will
choice_b: It is divided equally among all of the deceased sibling's next of kin
choice_d: It automatically passes to the surviving sibling, outside of probate
explanation: The defining feature of joint tenancy is the right of survivorship: when one joint tenant dies, that tenant's interest passes automatically and immediately to the surviving joint tenant(s) by operation of law, bypassing probate and any provision in a will.

question: A married couple takes title to their home in a form of ownership available only to spouses, which includes a right of survivorship and generally protects the property from being seized to satisfy the debt of only one spouse. This is known as:
explanation: Tenancy by the entirety is a special form of co-ownership available only to married couples in states that recognize it. Like joint tenancy it includes right of survivorship, but neither spouse can convey or encumber the property without the other's consent, and it often shields the property from an individual spouse's separate creditors.

question: A buyer purchases a unit within a multi-unit building and receives a deed granting exclusive ownership of the interior airspace of that unit, combined with an undivided tenancy-in-common interest, alongside all other unit owners, in the building's shared hallways, roof, and grounds. This describes:
explanation: Condominium ownership combines individual (fee simple) ownership of a specific unit's airspace with an undivided tenancy-in-common interest, shared with the other unit owners, in the building's common elements such as hallways, elevators, roof, and grounds.

question: A buyer purchases shares in a corporation that owns an entire apartment building, and in exchange receives a proprietary lease granting the right to occupy one specific unit in that building. This is an example of:
explanation: In cooperative ownership, a corporation holds title to the entire building, and residents purchase shares of stock in that corporation. Stock ownership entitles the shareholder to a proprietary lease granting the exclusive right to occupy a specific unit, rather than direct real property title to that unit.

question: A family purchases the right to use a beachfront condominium unit for one specific week every year, either owning that week outright or holding only a contractual right to use it. This arrangement is called:
choice_c: A tenancy in common with no survivorship
explanation: A timeshare divides the use of a property, typically a vacation unit, among multiple parties by allotted time periods. Timeshares may be structured as interval ownership (an actual, often fractional, ownership interest in the real estate) or as a right-to-use arrangement (a contractual license without a real property interest).

question: A grantor conveys a home to her elderly aunt 'for the aunt's lifetime,' after which the property is to pass to the grantor's daughter. What is the aunt's interest in the property called, and what happens to it when the aunt dies?
choice_a: A life estate; it automatically terminates at the aunt's death, and the property passes to the daughter as the remainderman
choice_b: A fee simple absolute; the aunt can pass it to her own heirs at death
choice_c: A leasehold estate that requires the aunt to pay rent
choice_d: A joint tenancy that gives the aunt permanent survivorship rights
explanation: A life estate grants ownership and use of property only for the duration of a specified person's life (the life tenant). Upon that person's death, the life estate automatically ends, and the property passes either back to the original grantor (a reversion) or to a third party named in the deed (a remainder, with that party called the remainderman).

question: A deed grants a life estate to Person A, but measures its duration by the lifetime of Person B rather than Person A's own lifetime. This unusual type of life estate is known as a life estate:
explanation: A life estate pur autre vie ('for the life of another') is a life estate whose duration is measured by the lifespan of someone other than the life tenant. If the life tenant dies before the measuring person, the estate passes to the life tenant's heirs until the measuring person's death.

question: A trustee holds legal title to real property for the benefit of another party under the terms of a written trust agreement. What is the interest held by the party who benefits from the trust called?
choice_d: A tenancy by the entirety interest
explanation: When property is held in trust, the trustee holds legal title and manages the property according to the trust document, while the beneficiary holds equitable (beneficial) title, meaning the right to receive the benefits of the property even though legal title is held by another.

question: A group of investors forms a limited liability company (LLC) to purchase and hold an apartment complex. Compared to holding the property as individual co-owners, which is a key advantage of taking title through the LLC?
choice_a: The property automatically passes to surviving members by right of survivorship
choice_b: An LLC cannot hold real property, only personal property
choice_c: Only married couples may form an LLC to hold real estate
choice_d: Members generally receive limited personal liability for the entity's debts and obligations while retaining flexible, pass-through tax treatment
explanation: Business entities such as corporations, partnerships, and limited liability companies can hold title to real property. An LLC is a popular choice because it typically shields members from personal liability for the entity's debts, similar to a corporation, while often allowing pass-through taxation similar to a partnership.

question: A commercial property is deeded to a corporation rather than to individual owners. Which characteristic of corporate ownership distinguishes it from ownership by a natural person?
choice_a: The corporation has perpetual existence and can hold title in severalty as a single legal entity, separate from its shareholders
choice_b: The corporation's ownership automatically terminates when any single shareholder dies
choice_c: A corporation cannot legally hold title to real property under any circumstances
choice_d: Corporate ownership always creates a tenancy in common among its shareholders
explanation: A corporation is a distinct legal entity that can hold title to real property in severalty in its own name. Because the corporation exists independently of its shareholders, it generally has perpetual (or indefinite) existence, and a shareholder's death does not affect the corporation's title to its property.
